claim: B-cell activation and immune synapse (IS) formation with membrane-bound antigens are actin-dependent processes.
source: B-cell activation and immune synapse (IS) formation with membrane-bound antigens are actin-dependent processes that scale positively with the strength of antigen-induced signals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior literature throughout the manuscript.

claim: B-cell activation and IS formation scale positively with the strength of antigen-induced signals.
source: B-cell activation and immune synapse (IS) formation with membrane-bound antigens are actin-dependent processes that scale positively with the strength of antigen-induced signals.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Ligating the B-cell integrin LFA-1 with ICAM-1 promotes IS formation when antigen is limiting.
source: Importantly, ligating the B-cell integrin, LFA-1, with ICAM-1 promotes IS formation when antigen is limiting.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to Carrasco et al., 2004 throughout the manuscript.

claim: LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions promote the formation of an actomyosin network that dominates the B-cell IS.
source: Here, we show using super-resolution imaging of mouse primary B cells that LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions promote the formation of an actomyosin network that dominates the B-cell IS.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The actomyosin network at the B-cell IS is created by the formin mDia1.
source: This network is created by the formin mDia1, organized into concentric, contractile arcs by myosin 2A, and flows inward at the same rate as B-cell receptor (BCR):antigen clusters.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using SMIFH2 (pan-formin inhibitor) and mDia1 miRNA knockdown shown in Figure 2.

claim: The actomyosin network is organized into concentric, contractile arcs by myosin 2A.
source: This network is created by the formin mDia1, organized into concentric, contractile arcs by myosin 2A, and flows inward at the same rate as B-cell receptor (BCR):antigen clusters.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing M2A co-localization with arcs (Figure 3) and disruption of arc organization by myosin inhibition (Figure 3F-H).

claim: The actomyosin network flows inward at the same rate as BCR:antigen clusters.
source: This network is created by the formin mDia1, organized into concentric, contractile arcs by myosin 2A, and flows inward at the same rate as B-cell receptor (BCR):antigen clusters.
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis and tracking data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual BCR microclusters are swept inward by individual actomyosin arcs.
source: Consistently, individual BCR microclusters are swept inward by individual actomyosin arcs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by high-magnification TIRF-SIM imaging showing arcs moving antigen clusters (Figure 4D-G, Video 10).

claim: Under conditions where integrin is required for synapse formation, inhibiting myosin impairs synapse formation.
source: Under conditions where integrin is required for synapse formation, inhibiting myosin impairs synapse formation, as evidenced by reduced antigen centralization, diminished BCR signaling, and defective signaling protein distribution at the synapse.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using pnBB (myosin inhibitor) under limiting antigen conditions shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Inhibiting myosin under integrin-dependent conditions reduces antigen centralization.
source: Under conditions where integrin is required for synapse formation, inhibiting myosin impairs synapse formation, as evidenced by reduced antigen centralization, diminished BCR signaling, and defective signaling protein distribution at the synapse.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of antigen distribution in pnBB-treated cells (Figure 5E-H).

claim: Inhibiting myosin under integrin-dependent conditions diminishes BCR signaling.
source: Under conditions where integrin is required for synapse formation, inhibiting myosin impairs synapse formation, as evidenced by reduced antigen centralization, diminished BCR signaling, and defective signaling protein distribution at the synapse.
evidence: This is shown by reduced P-CD79a and P-CD19 content in pnBB-treated cells (Figure 6C, F).

claim: Inhibiting myosin under integrin-dependent conditions causes defective signaling protein distribution at the synapse.
source: Under conditions where integrin is required for synapse formation, inhibiting myosin impairs synapse formation, as evidenced by reduced antigen centralization, diminished BCR signaling, and defective signaling protein distribution at the synapse.
evidence: This is demonstrated by altered distribution of P-CD79a and P-CD19 in pnBB-treated cells (Figure 6).

claim: A contractile actomyosin arc network plays a key role in the mechanism by which LFA-1 co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation and IS formation.
source: Together, these results argue that a contractile actomyosin arc network plays a key role in the mechanism by which LFA-1 co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation and IS formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BCR engagement with cognate antigen triggers striking changes in B-cell physiology that promote B-cell activation, immune synapse formation, and B-cell effector functions.
source: B-cell receptor (BCR) engagement with cognate antigen triggers striking changes in B-cell physiology that promote B-cell activation, immune synapse (IS) formation, and B-cell effector functions (Forthal, 2014; Heesters et al., 2016; Harwood and Batista, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by three citations to prior literature.

claim: BCR engagement triggers dramatic increases in actin filament assembly and dynamics that drive IS formation in B cells engaged with membrane-bound antigen.
source: These changes include dramatic increases in actin filament assembly and dynamics that are thought to drive IS formation in B cells engaged with membrane-bound antigen (Forthal, 2014; Heesters et al., 2016; Harwood and Batista, 2011; Gonzalez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by four citations to prior literature.

claim: For B cells in vivo, IS formation usually involves interactions with antigen bound to the surface of an antigen-presenting cell (APC).
source: For B cells in vivo, this usually involves interactions with antigen bound to the surface of an antigen-presenting cell (APC) (Gonzalez et al., 2011; Carrasco and Batista, 2006a; Cyster, 2010), although activating surfaces such as antigen-coated glass and planar lipid bilayers (PLBs) containing freely diffusing antigen are used to mimic these in vivo interactions.
evidence: This is supported by three citations to prior literature.

claim: IS formation is initiated by the formation of a radially symmetric, Arp2/3 complex-dependent branched actin network at the outer edge of the IS (in the dSMAC).
source: IS formation in these contexts is initiated by the formation of a radially symmetric, Arp2/3 complex-dependent branched actin network at the outer edge of the IS (i.e., in the distal supramolecular activation cluster [dSMAC]) (Wang and Hammer, 2020; Song et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by two citations to prior literature.

claim: The lamellipodia-like actin network in the dSMAC drives the spreading of the B cell across the antigen-coated surface, thereby promoting BCR:antigen interactions.
source: This lamellipodia-like actin network drives the spreading of the B cell across the antigen-coated surface, thereby promoting BCR:antigen interactions (Harwood and Batista, 2011; Fleire et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by two citations to prior literature.

claim: Once the B cell is fully spread, the continued polymerization of branched actin at the outer edge of the dSMAC generates a centripetal or retrograde flow of actin that drives the movement of BCR:antigen clusters towards the center of the synapse.
source: Once the B cell is fully spread, the continued polymerization of branched actin at the outer edge of the dSMAC generates a centripetal or retrograde flow of actin that drives the movement of BCR:antigen clusters (Tolar et al., 2009; Mattila et al., 2016; Treanor et al., 2009) towards the center of the synapse (i.e., to the central SMAC [cSMAC]) (Song et al., 2014; Bolger-Munro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by five citations to prior literature.

claim: Centripetal actin flow, combined with an overall contraction of the B cell, is thought to be responsible for the transport of BCR:antigen clusters to the center of the maturing synapse.
source: This centripetal actin flow, combined with an overall contraction of the B cell, is thought to be responsible for the transport of BCR:antigen clusters to the center of the maturing synapse (Bolger-Munro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by one citation to prior literature.

claim: The process of antigen centralization is required for robust BCR signaling.
source: Importantly, this process of antigen centralization is required for robust BCR signaling (Harwood and Batista, 2011; Mattila et al., 2016; Batista et al., 2010) and is thought to be a prerequisite for antigen internalization by follicular B cells (Batista et al., 2001; Yuseff et al., 2013; Yuseff and Lennon-Duménil, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by three citations to prior literature.

claim: Antigen centralization is thought to be a prerequisite for antigen internalization by follicular B cells.
source: Importantly, this process of antigen centralization is required for robust BCR signaling (Harwood and Batista, 2011; Mattila et al., 2016; Batista et al., 2010) and is thought to be a prerequisite for antigen internalization by follicular B cells (Batista et al., 2001; Yuseff et al., 2013; Yuseff and Lennon-Duménil, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by three citations to prior literature.

claim: Co-stimulatory signals can promote IS formation and B-cell activation when membrane-bound antigen binds the BCR weakly or is presented at low density.
source: Importantly, co-stimulatory signals can promote IS formation and B-cell activation under both of these conditions (Carrasco et al., 2004; Carrasco and Batista, 2006b).
evidence: This is supported by two citations to prior literature.

claim: The B-cell integrin LFA-1 binds the adhesion molecule ICAM-1 present on the surface of APCs.
source: Seminal work from Carrasco and colleagues showed that the B-cell integrin LFA-1, which binds the adhesion molecule ICAM-1 present on the surface of APCs (Springer, 1990; Springer et al., 1987), serves as one such co-stimulatory signal (Carrasco et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by two citations to prior literature.

claim: LFA-1 serves as a co-stimulatory signal for B-cell activation.
source: Seminal work from Carrasco and colleagues showed that the B-cell integrin LFA-1, which binds the adhesion molecule ICAM-1 present on the surface of APCs (Springer, 1990; Springer et al., 1987), serves as one such co-stimulatory signal (Carrasco et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carrasco et al., 2004.

claim: B cells respond robustly to higher affinity membrane-bound antigens presented at high density whether or not ICAM-1 is present on the membrane.
source: First, B cells responded robustly to higher affinity membrane-bound antigens presented at high density whether or not ICAM-1 was present on the membrane.
evidence: This is a finding from Carrasco et al., 2004 that is being summarized.

claim: The robust activation of B cells in response to antigens of all affinities increasingly required ICAM-1 in the membrane as the density of the antigen was lowered.
source: Second, the robust activation of B cells in response to antigens of all affinities increasingly required ICAM-1 in the membrane as the density of the antigen was lowered.
evidence: This is a finding from Carrasco et al., 2004 that is being summarized.

claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 was most dramatic for weaker antigens.
source: Third, this co-stimulatory effect was most dramatic for weaker antigens.
evidence: This is a finding from Carrasco et al., 2004 that is being summarized.

claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 was not observed in B cells lacking LFA-1.
source: Finally, this latter effect was not observed in B cells lacking LFA-1.
evidence: This is a finding from Carrasco et al., 2004 that is being summarized.

claim: LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions concentrate in the medial portion of the synapse (the pSMAC).
source: With regard to the underlying mechanism, IRM imaging suggested that LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions, which were shown to concentrate in the medial portion of the synapse (i.e., the peripheral SMAC [pSMAC]), lower the threshold for B-cell activation by enhancing cell adhesion.
evidence: This is based on findings from prior work being summarized.

claim: LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions lower the threshold for B-cell activation by enhancing cell adhesion.
source: With regard to the underlying mechanism, IRM imaging suggested that LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions, which were shown to concentrate in the medial portion of the synapse (i.e., the peripheral SMAC [pSMAC]), lower the threshold for B-cell activation by enhancing cell adhesion.
evidence: This is based on findings from prior work being summarized.

claim: The dendritic actin network occupying the outer dSMAC ring is thought to be the main driver of IS formation.
source: Relevant to this question, the dendritic actin network occupying the outer dSMAC ring, which is thought to be the main driver of IS formation, has been observed primarily in cells that received antigen stimulation alone and almost exclusively in immortalized B cell lines (Bolger-Munro et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Freeman et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by five citations to prior literature.

claim: The dendritic actin network in the dSMAC has been observed primarily in cells that received antigen stimulation alone and almost exclusively in immortalized B cell lines.
source: Relevant to this question, the dendritic actin network occupying the outer dSMAC ring, which is thought to be the main driver of IS formation, has been observed primarily in cells that received antigen stimulation alone and almost exclusively in immortalized B cell lines (Bolger-Munro et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Freeman et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by five citations to prior literature.

claim: Anti-IgM-engaged primary B cells exhibit a thin, bright, highly dynamic outer rim of F-actin that likely corresponds to the branched actin network comprising the dSMAC.
source: Individual video frames of anti-IgM-engaged B cells using both imaging modalities (Figure 1A and B), together with the corresponding videos (Video 1A and B), revealed a thin, bright, highly dynamic outer rim of F-actin (white arrows in Figure 1A and B) that likely corresponds to the branched actin network comprising the dSMAC (Bolger-Munro et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1A, B and Video 1, with interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The F-actin inside the outer dSMAC rim in anti-IgM-engaged cells is composed of a highly disorganized mixture of short-actin filaments/fibers and actin foci.
source: Both modalities (but especially TIRF-SIM) showed that the F-actin present inside this outer dSMAC rim is composed of a highly disorganized mixture of short-actin filaments/fibers and actin foci (blue brackets in Figure 1A and B), similarly to those observed previously in HeLa cells (Fritzsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1A, B, with comparison to prior work cited.

claim: Anti-IgM + ICAM-1-engaged B cells show a highly organized network inside the outer dSMAC rim (in the pSMAC) that is comprised of concentric actin arcs.
source: In sharp contrast, individual video frames of anti-IgM + ICAM-1-engaged B cells using both modalities (Figure 1C and D), together with the corresponding videos (Video 2A and B), showed a highly organized network inside the outer dSMAC rim (i.e., in the pSMAC) that is comprised of concentric actin arcs (blue brackets and magenta arrows in Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1C, D and Video 2.

claim: The addition of ICAM-1 increases the percentage of B cells with discernable arcs from ~30% to ~70%.
source: Consistently, scoring B cells for the presence of any discernable arcs showed that the addition of ICAM-1 increases the percentage of such cells from ~30% to ~70% (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The arcs in cells engaged with anti-IgM alone are sparse and transient.
source: Importantly, static and dynamic imaging showed that the arcs in cells engaged with anti-IgM alone are sparse and transient (Figure 1A and B, Video 1A and B), while those in cells engaged with both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 are dense and persistent (Figure 1C and D, Video 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1A, B and Video 1.

claim: The arcs in cells engaged with both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 are dense and persistent.
source: Importantly, static and dynamic imaging showed that the arcs in cells engaged with anti-IgM alone are sparse and transient (Figure 1A and B, Video 1A and B), while those in cells engaged with both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 are dense and persistent (Figure 1C and D, Video 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1C, D and Video 2.

claim: Measuring the degree of alignment between actin filaments in the pSMAC revealed a large shift towards more organized pSMAC actin when ICAM-1 was included.
source: Consistently, measuring the degree of alignment between actin filaments in the pSMAC portion of B cells stimulated with anti-IgM alone versus both anti-IgM and ICAM-1, which were made using FibrilTool (Boudaoud et al., 2014), revealed a large shift towards more organized pSMAC actin when ICAM-1 was included (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A1–A3; see the figure legend for details).
evidence: This is based on quantification using FibrilTool shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The actin arc-containing pSMAC comprises the major actin network at the IS of primary B cells engaged using both anti-IgM and ICAM-1.
source: Finally, measuring the percentage of total synaptic F-actin content within each SMAC (Figure 1H), and the percentage of total IS footprint occupied by each SMAC (Figure 1I), showed that the actin arc-containing pSMAC comprises the major actin network at the IS of primary B cells engaged using both anti-IgM and ICAM-1.
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: Primary B cells stimulated with anti-IgM and ICAM-1 exhibit small, actin-rich surface spikes at the outer synapse edge.
source: Primary B cells stimulated in this way exhibit small, actin-rich surface spikes at the outer synapse edge (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The actin within surface spikes continues into the cytoplasm in the form of linear actin filaments.
source: Importantly, magnified images revealed that the actin within these spikes continues into the cytoplasm in the form of linear actin filaments (Figure 2B1 and B2).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2B1 and B2.

claim: Linear actin filaments nucleated at the plasma membrane at the outer edge of the synapse are contiguous with the pSMAC actin arcs.
source: Moreover, tracing these linear actin filaments showed that they are contiguous with the pSMAC actin arcs (Figure 2C1 and C2, Video 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2C1, C2 and Video 3.

claim: Linear actin filaments nucleated at the plasma membrane at the outer edge of the synapse give rise to the actin arcs populating the pSMAC.
source: These results argue that linear actin filaments nucleated at the plasma membrane at the outer edge of the synapse give rise to the actin arcs populating the pSMAC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the imaging data showing continuity between linear filaments and arcs.

claim: The specific nucleator creating the linear actin filaments is likely a member of the formin family based on the fact that the actin being made is linear and nucleated at the plasma membrane.
source: While these results do not identify the specific nucleator involved, they do point to it being a member of the formin family based on the fact that the actin being made is linear and nucleated at the plasma membrane (Goode and Eck, 2007; Breitsprecher and Goode, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of formins cited in the literature.

claim: Formins incorporate fluorescent protein-labeled actin monomer into filaments poorly.
source: Consistent with this conjecture, and with the fact that formins incorporate fluorescent protein-labeled actin monomer into filaments poorly (Yi et al., 2012; Murugesan et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2012), we did not see fluorescent actin arcs in B cells expressing mEOS-labeled G-actin (Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by three citations and by imaging data shown in Video 4.

claim: B cells expressing mEOS-labeled G-actin do not show fluorescent actin arcs.
source: Consistent with this conjecture, and with the fact that formins incorporate fluorescent protein-labeled actin monomer into filaments poorly (Yi et al., 2012; Murugesan et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2012), we did not see fluorescent actin arcs in B cells expressing mEOS-labeled G-actin (Video 4).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Video 4.

claim: The pSMAC actin arcs present in a primary B cell largely disappeared 6 min after adding SMIFH2.
source: Figure 2D1 and D2, together with the line scan in Figure 2E, show that the pSMAC actin arcs present in a representative primary B cell immediately before SMIFH2 addition (blue trace) had largely disappeared 6 min after adding SMIFH2 (magenta trace).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2D1, D2, and E.

claim: A20 B cells expressing each of three different mDia1 miRNAs were largely devoid of actin arcs compared to control A20 B cells.
source: Compared to control A20 B cells (Figure 2F1), representative B cells expressing each of the three miRNAs (Figure 2F2–F4) were largely devoid of actin arcs.
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2F1-F4.

claim: The ratio of pSMAC to dSMAC F-actin and the amount of F-actin in the pSMAC support that mDia1 knockdown reduces actin arcs.
source: This difference was supported by quantitating the ratio of pSMAC to dSMAC F-actin (Figure 2G), as well as the amount of F-actin in the pSMAC (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2G and 2H.

claim: Actin arcs were unaffected by the expression of two different nontargeting miRNAs.
source: Finally, actin arcs were unaffected by the expression of two different nontargeting miRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C1–C4 and D1–D4).
evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The pSMAC actin arcs are created by a formin, and the formin mDia1 likely plays a major role.
source: Together, these results argue that the pSMAC actin arcs are indeed created by a formin, and that the formin mDia1 likely plays a major role.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMIFH2 and mDia1 knockdown experiments.

claim: CK-666 addition leads to a reduction in the size of the dSMAC and an increase in arc content in the pSMAC.
source: Consistently, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1/A2 (before CK-666 addition) and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A3/A4 (after CK-666 addition) together show that CK-666 addition leads not only to a reduction in the size of the dSMAC (magenta brackets), but also to an increase in arc content in the pSMAC (blue brackets).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Following CK-666 treatment, there is a significant shift away from dSMAC F-actin and toward pSMAC F-actin.
source: These changes were supported by measuring the percentage of total synaptic F-actin content residing within each SMAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), which revealed a significant shift away from dSMAC F-actin and toward pSMAC F-actin following CK-666 treatment.
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The shift in F-actin distribution following CK-666 treatment was reflected in measurements of total pSMAC F-actin content, the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC F-actin content, and the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC area.
source: This shift was also reflected in measurements of total pSMAC F-actin content (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC F-actin content (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), and the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC area (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Linear actin filaments generated by the formin mDia1 at the outer edge of the synapse give rise to the pSMAC actin arc network.
source: Taken together, these data argue strongly that linear actin filaments generated by the formin mDia1 at the outer edge of the synapse give rise to the pSMAC actin arc network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data on formin inhibition, mDia1 knockdown, and Arp2/3 inhibition.

claim: Formin-derived linear actin filaments are commonly organized into well-defined structures such as stress fibers, transverse arcs, and the contractile ring in dividing cells by bipolar filaments of myosin 2.
source: Formin-derived linear actin filaments are commonly organized into well-defined structures such as stress fibers, transverse arcs, and the contractile ring in dividing cells by bipolar filaments of the actin-based motor protein myosin 2 (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Sellers, 2000; Shutova and Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by three citations to prior literature.

claim: M2A is the only myosin 2 isoform expressed in B cells.
source: To define the localization and dynamics of myosin 2 at the B-cell IS, we used primary B cells isolated from a mouse in which GFP had been knocked into the N- terminus of the myosin 2A heavy chain gene Myh9 (referred to herein as M2A) (Zhang et al., 2012) as M2A is the only myosin 2 isoform expressed in B cells (ImmGen Database).
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on the ImmGen Database.

claim: M2A co-localizes dramatically with the actin arcs in the pSMAC.
source: Individual video frames of these cells following transfection with Td-Tomato-F-Tractin and attachment to coverslips coated with anti-IgM and ICAM-1 revealed a dramatic co-localization between M2A and the actin arcs in the pSMAC (Figure 3A1–A3, Video 6).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3A1-A3 and Video 6.

claim: The myosin signals align with actin arcs in a periodic fashion that resembles other myosin 2-rich, linear actin structures like stress fibers and the contractile ring.
source: Magnified TIRF-SIM images show that the myosin signals align with actin arcs in a periodic fashion (Figure 3A4) that resembles other myosin 2-rich, linear actin structures like stress fibers and the contractile ring (Beach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3A4, with comparison to prior work cited.

claim: The myosin signals exhibit the SIM signature for M2A bipolar filaments when M2A is GFP-labeled at its N-terminus, which is a pair of GFP puncta spaced ~300 nm apart.
source: Moreover, these myosin signals exhibit the SIM signature for M2A bipolar filaments when M2A is GFP-labeled at its N-terminus (Beach et al., 2017), which is a pair of GFP puncta spaced ~300 nm apart (Figure 3A5; 304 ± 32 nm; n = 230 filaments from 12 cells).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3A5 and quantification, with comparison to prior work cited.

claim: The presence of M2A filaments in the medial portion of the synapse was evident in primary B cells isolated from a mouse in which mCherry had been knocked into the N-terminus of M2A.
source: The presence of M2A filaments in the medial portion of the synapse was also evident in primary B cells isolated from a mouse in which mCherry had been knocked into the N-terminus of M2A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), primary B cells that we genome-edited using CRISPR to place GFP at the N-terminus of M2A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and A20 B cells that we genome edited using CRISPR to place mScarleti at the N-terminus of M2A and then transfected with GFP-F-Tractin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C1–C3, Video 5B).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C and Video 5B.

claim: 3D-SIM images of fixed and stained A20 B cells showed that endogenous M2A co-localizes with the actin arcs.
source: Finally, 3D-SIM images of A20 B cells that were fixed and stained for M2A and F-actin showed that endogenous M2A also co-localizes with the actin arcs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D1–D3; note that the signature for M2A filaments using this antibody, which recognizes the C-terminus of M2A, is a single fluorescent punctum that corresponds to the center of an individual M2A filament) (Beach et al., 2014; Beach and Hammer, 2015).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D1-D3, with explanation supported by citations.

claim: The actin arc network in primary B cells receiving ICAM-1 co-stimulation is an actomyosin arc network.
source: Together, these results show that the actin arc network in primary B cells receiving ICAM-1 co-stimulation is in fact an actomyosin arc network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-localization data.

claim: Bipolar filaments of M2A begin to appear near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary in association with the linear actin filaments/bundles exiting the dSMAC.
source: Individual video frames (Figure 3B1–B6), as well as the corresponding video (Video 7), show that bipolar filaments of M2A begin to appear near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary in association with the linear actin filaments/bundles exiting the dSMAC (white, yellow, and fuchsia arrowheads mark such myosin filaments at time 0 s in Figure 3B1).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B1-B6 and Video 7.

claim: As time progresses, M2A filaments move centripetally and undergo expansion into filament clusters.
source: As time progresses, these filaments move centripetally and undergo expansion into filament clusters (Figure 3B1–B6; see also Video 7).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B1-B6 and Video 7.

claim: The expansion of M2A filaments into clusters is presumably driven by the same sequential amplification pathway described previously for M2A filament assembly in fibroblasts.
source: This expansion, in which individual myosin filaments expand into a small cluster of filaments, is presumably driven by the same sequential amplification pathway described previously for M2A filament assembly in fibroblasts (Beach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to prior work cited.

claim: The myosin filaments in M2A clusters begin to align with the arcs forming at the outer edge of the pSMAC, which then merge with the larger actomyosin arc network in the pSMAC.
source: Finally, the myosin filaments in these clusters begin to align with the arcs forming at the outer edge of the pSMAC, which then merge with the larger actomyosin arc network in the pSMAC (Figure 3B1–B6).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B1-B6.

claim: New myosin filaments keep appearing near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary to repeat the process of assembly and organization.
source: As all this is happening, new myosin filaments keep appearing near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary to repeat the process (Figure 3B2–B6; follow the blue, green, and purple arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B2-B6.

claim: Primary GFP-M2A knockin B cells receiving both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 stimulation exhibited a greater amount of synaptic M2A than B cells receiving only anti-IgM stimulation.
source: Consistently, primary GFP-M2A knockin B cells receiving both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 stimulation exhibited a greater amount of synaptic M2A than B cells receiving only anti-IgM stimulation (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The difference in synaptic M2A between cells receiving anti-IgM alone versus anti-IgM + ICAM-1 remained significant even after normalizing for cell-spread area.
source: Of note, this difference remained significant even after normalizing the M2A fluorescence for a small difference in the average cell-spread area under these two conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G1–G2).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G1-G2.

claim: Cells treated with 25 μM pnBB displayed highly disorganized, mesh-like actin arrays in their pSMAC, while control DMSO-treated cells exhibited concentric actin arcs.
source: While control, DMSO-treated cells exhibited concentric actin arcs in their pSMAC as expected (Figure 3F), cells treated with 25 μM pnBB displayed highly disorganized, mesh-like actin arrays in their pSMAC (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Anisotropy measurements revealed a dramatic shift towards more disorganized pSMAC actin when B cells are treated with pnBB.
source: Consistently, anisotropy measurements made using FibrilTool revealed a dramatic shift towards more disorganized pSMAC actin when B cells are treated with pnBB (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 3H.

claim: M2A contractility is required for the concentric organization of the pSMAC actin arcs.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that M2A contractility is indeed required for the concentric organization of the pSMAC actin arcs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pnBB treatment experiments.

claim: B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM and ICAM-1 generated significantly more traction force than B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM alone.
source: As expected (Wang, 2018; Kumari et al., 2019), B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM and ICAM-1 generated significantly more traction force than B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A1, A2, B1, B2, and D).
evidence: This is based on traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, with comparison to prior work cited.

claim: ICAM-1-dependent traction forces were completely abrogated by pretreating the cells with pnBB.
source: Importantly, ICAM-1-dependent traction forces were completely abrogated by pretreating the cells with pnBB (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C1, C2, and D), indicating that the generation of integrin-dependent traction forces requires M2A contractility.
evidence: This is based on traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The generation of integrin-dependent traction forces requires M2A contractility.
source: Importantly, ICAM-1-dependent traction forces were completely abrogated by pretreating the cells with pnBB (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C1, C2, and D), indicating that the generation of integrin-dependent traction forces requires M2A contractility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pnBB treatment experiments on traction forces.

claim: The requirement for M2A contractility in traction force generation likely reflects pulling forces exerted by M2A on the substrate through LFA-1:ICAM-1 pairs, combined with the increase in M2A content at the synapse caused by ligating LFA-1 with ICAM-1, and the contribution that M2A-dependent pulling forces make in keeping LFA-1 in its open, active conformation.
source: This requirement likely reflects pulling forces exerted by M2A on the substrate through LFA-1:ICAM-1 pairs, combined with the increase in M2A content at the synapse caused by ligating LFA-1 with ICAM-1, and the contribution that M2A-dependent pulling forces make in keeping LFA-1 in its open, active conformation (Gardel et al., 2010; Case and Waterman, 2015; Comrie and Burkhardt, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism supported by three citations to prior literature.

claim: Integrin clusters are known to accumulate in the pSMAC portion of the B-cell IS.
source: These results, together with the fact that integrin clusters are known to accumulate in the pSMAC portion of the B-cell IS (Carrasco et al., 2004; Carrasco and Batista, 2006b), suggest a feed-forward relationship where integrin ligation promotes the formation of pSMAC actomyosin arcs, and the contractile forces exerted by these actomyosin arcs promote further integrin activation and robust adhesion in the pSMAC.
evidence: This is stated as known fact supported by two citations.

claim: There is a feed-forward relationship where integrin ligation promotes the formation of pSMAC actomyosin arcs, and the contractile forces exerted by these actomyosin arcs promote further integrin activation and robust adhesion in the pSMAC.
source: These results, together with the fact that integrin clusters are known to accumulate in the pSMAC portion of the B-cell IS (Carrasco et al., 2004; Carrasco and Batista, 2006b), suggest a feed-forward relationship where integrin ligation promotes the formation of pSMAC actomyosin arcs, and the contractile forces exerted by these actomyosin arcs promote further integrin activation and robust adhesion in the pSMAC.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data and prior knowledge.

claim: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network flows centripetally at 1.07 ± 0.07 µm/min in primary B cells.
source: Kymograph analyses of actin flow across synapses made by primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin showed that their pSMAC actomyosin arc network indeed flows centripetally at 1.07 ± 0.07 µm/min, or about one-third the rate of centripetal actin flow in the dSMAC (2.89 ± 0.18 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1-A3.

claim: The dSMAC exhibits centripetal actin flow at 2.89 ± 0.18 µm/min in primary B cells.
source: Kymograph analyses of actin flow across synapses made by primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin showed that their pSMAC actomyosin arc network indeed flows centripetally at 1.07 ± 0.07 µm/min, or about one-third the rate of centripetal actin flow in the dSMAC (2.89 ± 0.18 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1-A3.

claim: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network flows centripetally at 0.97 ± 0.13 µm/min in A20 B cells.
source: Similar results were obtained for A20 B cells (pSMAC rate: 0.97 ± 0.13 µm/min; dSMAC rate: 3.16 ± 0.35 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1–B3).
evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1-B3.

claim: The dSMAC exhibits centripetal actin flow at 3.16 ± 0.35 µm/min in A20 B cells.
source: Similar results were obtained for A20 B cells (pSMAC rate: 0.97 ± 0.13 µm/min; dSMAC rate: 3.16 ± 0.35 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1–B3).
evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1-B3.

claim: The actomyosin arcs could contribute along with the branched actin network in the dSMAC to the inward transport of BCR:antigen clusters.
source: Together, these results indicate that the actomyosin arcs could contribute along with the branched actin network in the dSMAC to the inward transport of BCR:antigen clusters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the centripetal flow data.

claim: Primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin readily formed actin arcs when PLBs contained both anti-IgM and ICAM-1, but not when they contained anti-IgM alone.
source: As expected, primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin readily formed actin arcs when PLBs contained both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 (Video 8A), but not when they contained anti-IgM alone (Video 8B).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Video 8A and 8B.

claim: Primary B cells engaged with PLBs containing fluorescent anti-IgM and unlabeled ICAM-1 yielded mature synapses in which concentric actin arcs surrounded antigen accumulated in the cSMAC.
source: Also as expected, primary B cells engaged with PLBs containing fluorescent anti-IgM (magenta) and unlabeled ICAM-1 yielded mature synapses in which concentric actin arcs surrounded antigen accumulated in the cSMAC (Figure 4A1–A3, white arrows).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 4A1-A3.

claim: Single-antigen microclusters moved inward at 2.36 ± 1.1 µm/min across the dSMAC and 1.03 ± 0.3 µm/min across the pSMAC.
source: Tracking of single-antigen microclusters showed that they moved inward at 2.36 ± 1.1 µm/min and 1.03 ± 0.3 µm/min across the dSMAC (magenta tracks) and pSMAC (green tracks), respectively (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on tracking data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The rates of antigen microcluster movement are very similar to the rates of centripetal actin flow across the dSMAC and pSMAC.
source: Importantly, these rates are very similar to the rates of centripetal actin flow across the dSMAC and pSMAC, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
evidence: This is a comparison between the antigen tracking data and the actin flow data.

claim: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network works together with the dSMAC branched actin network to drive antigen centralization.
source: Together, these observations argue that the pSMAC actomyosin arc network works together with the dSMAC branched actin network to drive antigen centralization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similarity in rates between actin flow and antigen movement.

claim: Individual actin arcs move individual BCR:antigen microclusters inward via a sweeping mechanism that likely depends on frictional coupling between the actin arc and microcluster.
source: Together, these results argue that individual actin arcs move individual BCR:antigen microclusters inward via a sweeping mechanism that likely depends on frictional coupling between the actin arc and microcluster (Yu et al., 2010; Ditlev et al., 2019; Smoligovets et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from high-magnification imaging data, with mechanism supported by three citations.

claim: The overall incidence of arcs slipping past microclusters must be fairly small as the rate of inward antigen transport across the pSMAC is not significantly slower than the rate of inward actin arc flow across the pSMAC.
source: While arcs can slip past microclusters, the overall incidence of such slippage must be fairly small as the rate of inward antigen transport across the pSMAC (Figure 4C) is not significantly slower than the rate of inward actin arc flow across the pSMAC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the rates of antigen movement and actin flow.

claim: B cells engaged with membrane-bound antigen at low density fail to centralize antigen unless their integrin LFA-1 is also engaged with ICAM-1 in the target membrane.
source: B cells engaged with membrane-bound antigen at low density fail to centralize antigen unless their integrin LFA-1 is also engaged with ICAM-1 in the target membrane (Carrasco et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a known finding supported by citation to Carrasco et al., 2004.

claim: B cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation over 10 min without the need for ICAM-1 when the PLB was loaded with anti-IgM at 2 µg/ml (high-density antigen).
source: B cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation over 10 min without the need for ICAM-1 when the PLB was loaded using a solution containing anti-IgM at a concentration of 2 µg/ml (hereafter referred to as 'high-density antigen') (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A1-A3.

claim: B cells formed antigen microclusters across their synaptic interface but failed to centralize them over 10 min when the PLB was loaded with anti-IgM at 0.15 µg/ml (low or limiting density antigen).
source: By contrast, B cells formed antigen microclusters across their synaptic interface but failed to centralize them over 10 min when the PLB was loaded using a solution containing anti-IgM at a concentration 0.15 µg/ml (hereafter referred to as 'low or limiting density antigen') (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B1–B3).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B1-B3.

claim: When unlabeled ICAM-1 was included in low-density antigen bilayers, B cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation.
source: Importantly, when unlabeled ICAM-1 was included in these low-density antigen bilayers, B cells now exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C1–C3).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C1-C3.

claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 on antigen centralization was supported by scoring antigen distribution as centralized, partially centralized or noncentralized.
source: This co-stimulatory effect was supported by scoring antigen distribution as centralized, partially centralized or noncentralized (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D1–D3 and E).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 was supported by scoring the percent of total synaptic antigen present within the cSMAC.
source: It was also supported by scoring the percent of total synaptic antigen present within the cSMAC, which was defined by a circular area encompassing 20% of the entire synaptic interface and centered around the center of mass of the fluorescent antigen-containing pixels within the interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 was supported by measuring the size of antigen clusters as a function of their distance from the center of the cSMAC.
source: Finally, it was supported by measuring the size of antigen clusters as a function of their distance from the center of the cSMAC (defined as above) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: B cells engaged with PLBs containing antigen at the limiting density and no ICAM-1 exhibited small antigen clusters (~0.3 µm2) located roughly evenly across the synaptic interface.
source: Specifically, B cells engaged with PLBs containing antigen at the limiting density and no ICAM-1 exhibited small antigen clusters (~0.3 µm2) located roughly evenly across the synaptic interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, black trace), while B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 in addition to antigen at the limiting density exhibited large antigen clusters (up to 3 µm2), the largest of which were located at the center of the cSMAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, green trace).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 in addition to antigen at the limiting density exhibited large antigen clusters (up to 3 µm2), the largest of which were located at the center of the cSMAC.
source: Specifically, B cells engaged with PLBs containing antigen at the limiting density and no ICAM-1 exhibited small antigen clusters (~0.3 µm2) located roughly evenly across the synaptic interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, black trace), while B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 in addition to antigen at the limiting density exhibited large antigen clusters (up to 3 µm2), the largest of which were located at the center of the cSMAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, green trace).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was greater for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM + ICAM-1 than for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM alone.
source: Of note, the total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was also greater for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM + ICAM-1 than for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: DMSO-treated cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation when engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and anti-IgM at the limiting density.
source: While DMSO-treated cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation (Figure 5A1–A3), pnBB-treated cells failed to centralize antigen/create a cSMAC (Figure 5B1–B3).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5A1-A3.

claim: pnBB-treated cells failed to centralize antigen/create a cSMAC when engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and anti-IgM at the limiting density.
source: While DMSO-treated cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation (Figure 5A1–A3), pnBB-treated cells failed to centralize antigen/create a cSMAC (Figure 5B1–B3).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5B1-B3.

claim: The actin arcs that surround centralized antigen in DMSO-treated cells were absent in pnBB-treated cells.
source: Consistently, the actin arcs that surround centralized antigen in DMSO-treated cells (Figure 5C1–C3, white arrows) were absent in pnBB-treated cells (Figure 5D1–D3).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5C1-C3 and 5D1-D3.

claim: Myosin inhibition abrogates the integrin co-stimulatory effect on antigen centralization.
source: The fact that myosin inhibition abrogates the integrin co-stimulatory effect was further supported by scoring antigen distribution in control and pnBB-treated cells as centralized, partially centralized, or noncentralized (Figure 5E), byscoring the percent of total synaptic antigen present within the cSMAC (Figure 5F), and bymeasuring the size of antigen clusters as a function of their distance from the center of the cSMAC (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: The total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was greater for cells treated with DMSO than for cells treated with pnBB.
source: Of note, the total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was also greater for cells treated with DMSO than for cells treated with pnBB (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The ability of integrin ligation to promote antigen centralization and cSMAC formation when antigen is limiting requires myosin contractility.
source: Together, these results show that the ability of integrin ligation to promote antigen centralization and cSMAC formation when antigen is limiting requires myosin contractility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pnBB treatment experiments under limiting antigen conditions.

claim: The contractile actomyosin arc network created downstream of integrin ligation plays an important role in the mechanism by which LFA-1 co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation.
source: This in turn argues that the contractile actomyosin arc network created downstream of integrin ligation plays an important role in the mechanism by which LFA-1 co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data on myosin's role in integrin-dependent IS formation.

claim: DMSO-treated primary B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and limiting antigen exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD79a and anti-IgM concentrated in the cSMAC.
source: Consistent with results above and with the known properties of CD79a, DMSO-treated primary B cells engaged for 10 min with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and limiting antigen and then fixed/stained for P-CD79a exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD79a and anti-IgM concentrated in the cSMAC (Figure 6A1–A4).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6A1-A4.

claim: pnBB-treated B cells failed to form a clear cSMAC, resulting in CD79a and anti-IgM spread across the synapse.
source: Also as expected, pnBB-treated B cells failed to form a clear cSMAC, resulting in CD79a and anti-IgM spread across the synapse (Figure 6B1–B4).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6B1-B4.

claim: pnBB-treated cells exhibited a significant reduction relative to control cells in synaptic P-CD79a content.
source: Importantly, quantitation showed that pnBB-treated cells also exhibited a significant reduction relative to control cells in synaptic P-CD79a content (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The defect in synaptic P-CD79a content was also seen after only 5 min on PLBs.
source: This defect was also seen after only 5 min on PLBs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and the defects at both time points were not due to differences between BB-treated cells and control cells in synaptic CD79a content (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The defects in P-CD79a at 5 and 10 min were not due to differences between BB-treated cells and control cells in synaptic CD79a content.
source: This defect was also seen after only 5 min on PLBs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and the defects at both time points were not due to differences between BB-treated cells and control cells in synaptic CD79a content (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DMSO-treated primary B cells exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD19 enriched at the outer edge of the IgM concentrated in the cSMAC.
source: DMSO-treated primary B cells engaged with PLBs as above exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD19 enriched at the outer edge of the IgM concentrated in the cSMAC (Figure 6D1–D4).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6D1-D4.

claim: The enrichment of P-CD19 at the pSMAC/cSMAC boundary was confirmed by line scans of the fluorescence intensities for F-actin, anti-IgM, and P-CD19.
source: This enrichment of P-CD19 at the pSMAC/cSMAC boundary was confirmed by line scans of the fluorescence intensities for F-actin, anti-IgM, and P-CD19 (Figure 6G, see boxed pSMAC regions).
evidence: This is based on line scan analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: In contrast to control cells, pnBB-treated B cells failed to concentrate anti-IgM at the center of the synapse, and P-CD19 staining was spread across the synaptic interface.
source: In contrast to control cells, pnBB-treated B cells failed to concentrate anti-IgM at the center of the synapse, and P-CD19 staining was now spread across the synaptic interface (Figure 6E1–E4 and H).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6E1-E4 and line scan analysis in Figure 6H.

claim: pnBB-treated cells exhibited a significant reduction relative to control cells in synaptic P-CD19 content.
source: Moreover, quantitation showed that pnBB-treated cells also exhibited a significant reduction relative to control cells in synaptic P-CD19 content (Figure 6F) that was not due to a difference in synaptic CD19 content (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The reduction in synaptic P-CD19 content in pnBB-treated cells was not due to a difference in synaptic CD19 content.
source: Moreover, quantitation showed that pnBB-treated cells also exhibited a significant reduction relative to control cells in synaptic P-CD19 content (Figure 6F) that was not due to a difference in synaptic CD19 content (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The actomyosin arcs promote BCR-dependent signaling.
source: Together, these results indicate that the actomyosin arcs promote BCR-dependent signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of myosin inhibition on P-CD79a and P-CD19.

claim: Recent studies have presented evidence that GC B cells differ markedly from naïve B cells with regard to the distribution and fate of antigen at mature synapses.
source: Recent studies have presented evidence that GC B cells differ markedly from naïve B cells with regard to the distribution and fate of antigen at mature synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of recent findings.

claim: Rather than concentrating antigen at the center of the synapse and using actomyosin force to extract it there, GC B cells accumulate antigen in clusters at the periphery of the synapse and use actomyosin force to extract it there.
source: Rather than concentrating antigen at the center of the synapse and using actomyosin force to extract it there, GC B cells accumulate antigen in clusters at the periphery of the synapse and use actomyosin force to extract it there (Hammer et al., 2019; Nowosad et al., 2016; Kwak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by three citations to prior literature.

claim: TIRF-SIM imaging of mouse GC B cells isolated from the GFP-M2A knockin mouse revealed a subset of cells exhibiting enrichment of M2A filaments in the medial, pSMAC portion of the synapse.
source: Consistently, TIRF-SIM imaging of mouse GC B cells isolated from the GFP-M2A knockin mouse that were stained with CellMask Deep Red and plated on coverslips coated with anti-IgM, anti-IgG, and ICAM-1 revealed a subset of cells exhibiting enrichment of M2A filaments in the medial, pSMAC portion of the synapse (Video 11), just as in naïve B cells.
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Video 11.

claim: M2A filaments in GC B cells move centripetally.
source: Moreover, these myosin filaments move centripetally (Video 11) and co-localize with pSMAC actin arcs in phalloidin-stained samples (Figure 7A1–A3, white arrows), just as in naïve B cells.
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Video 11.

claim: M2A filaments in GC B cells co-localize with pSMAC actin arcs in phalloidin-stained samples.
source: Moreover, these myosin filaments move centripetally (Video 11) and co-localize with pSMAC actin arcs in phalloidin-stained samples (Figure 7A1–A3, white arrows), just as in naïve B cells.
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 7A1-A3.

claim: About one-third of GC B cells exhibited robust accumulation of M2A filaments in the pSMAC when engaged with anti-IgM/IgG-coated glass.
source: Importantly, scoring showed that about one-third of GC B cells exhibited robust accumulation of M2A filaments in the pSMAC when engaged with anti-IgM/IgG-coated glass (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 7B.

claim: About one-third of GC B cells engaged for 10 min with PLBs containing fluorophore-labeled anti-IgM/IgG and unlabeled ICAM-1 exhibited robust accumulation of M2A filaments in the pSMAC.
source: Similarly, about one-third of GC B cells engaged for 10 min with PLBs containing fluorophore-labeled anti-IgM/IgG and unlabeled ICAM-1, and then fixed and stained with phalloidin, exhibited robust accumulation of M2A filaments in the pSMAC (Figure 7C1–C4 and D,).
evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7C1-C4 and 7D.

claim: Actomyosin arcs in GC B cells can be seen to surround antigen accumulated at the center of the synapse.
source: Importantly, these actomyosin arcs can be seen to surround antigen accumulated at the center of the synapse (see the white arrows in Figure 7C1, C2, and C4).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 7C1, C2, and C4.

claim: Actomyosin arcs can contribute to antigen centralization in GC B cells as well as in naïve B cells.
source: This finding, together with the fact that the myosin moves centripetally during IS formation (Video 11), suggests that actomyosin arcs can contribute to antigen centralization in GC B cells as well as in naïve B cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the imaging data on GC B cells.

claim: ~45% of GC B cell synapses exhibited small to medium-sized antigen clusters distributed to varying degrees in the synapse periphery.
source: In partial agreement with previous findings (Nowosad et al., 2016; Kwak et al., 2018), ~45% of synapses exhibited small to medium-sized antigen clusters distributed to varying degrees in the synapse periphery (Figure 7E1, E2, and F).
evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7E1, E2, and F.

claim: ~20% of GC B cell synapses exhibited antigen microclusters spread throughout the synaptic interface.
source: In addition, ~20% of synapses exhibited antigen microclusters spread throughout the synaptic interface (Figure 7E3 and F).
evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7E3 and F.

claim: ~35% of GC B cell synapses exhibited highly centralized antigen.
source: Importantly, the remaining ~35% of synapses exhibited highly centralized antigen (Figure 7E4 and F).
evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7E4 and F.

claim: GC B cell synapses with centralized antigen showed a pSMAC-like accumulation of GFP-M2A surrounding much of the centralized antigen.
source: Images of these synapses showed a pSMAC-like accumulation of GFP-M2A surrounding much of the centralized antigen (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A1; see also Video 12).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A1 and Video 12.

claim: GC B cell synapses containing either peripheral antigen clusters or microclusters showed no obvious pattern to the distribution of GFP-M2A.
source: Conversely, images of synapses containing either peripheral antigen clusters or microclusters showed no obvious pattern to the distribution of GFP-M2A (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A2 and A3; see also Video 13).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A2, A3 and Video 13.

claim: GC B cell synapses containing peripheral antigen clusters exhibited less total GFP-M2A signal than the synapses with centralized antigen.
source: Moreover, the synapses containing peripheral antigen clusters exhibited less total GFP-M2A signal than the synapses with centralized antigen (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), and the signals appeared more transient (compare Video 13 to Video 12).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and comparison of videos.

claim: GC B cells with centralized antigen (about one-third of cells) are the ones that make actomyosin arcs (again, about one-third of cells).
source: These results, together with the images in Figure 7C1–C4, argue that GC B cells with centralized antigen (about one-third of cells) are the ones that make actomyosin arcs (again, about one-third of cells).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between centralized antigen and M2A accumulation.

claim: GC B cells can make actomyosin arcs and likely use this structure to centralize antigen, although the degree to which they do this is considerably less than for naïve B cells.
source: We conclude, therefore, that GC B cells can make actomyosin arcs and that they likely use this structure to centralize antigen, although the degree to which they do this is considerably less than for naïve B cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GC B cell imaging data.

claim: Integrin co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation and synapse formation when antigen is limiting by promoting B-cell adhesion.
source: Integrin co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation and IS formation when antigen is limiting by promoting B-cell adhesion (Carrasco et al., 2004; Carrasco and Batista, 2006b).
evidence: This is stated as a known finding supported by two citations.

claim: Integrin co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation and synapse formation not only by enhancing B-cell adhesion, but also by eliciting the formation of a contractile actomyosin arc network that drives mechanical force-dependent IS formation.
source: Together, our results argue that integrin co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation and synapse formation not only by enhancing B-cell adhesion (Carrasco et al., 2004), but also by eliciting the formation of a contractile actomyosin arc network that drives mechanical force-dependent IS formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript based on the collective data.

claim: Most in vitro studies of B-cell IS formation and activation have been performed under conditions of excess antigen, while antigen is rarely available in excess in vivo.
source: This reset is especially important given that most in vitro studies of B-cell IS formation and activation have been performed under conditions of excess antigen, while antigen is rarely available in excess in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the importance of the findings.

claim: A central player in the link between integrin co-stimulation and the formation of the actomyosin arc network is almost certainly active RhoA.
source: A central player in the link between integrin co-stimulation and the formation of the actomyosin arc network is almost certainly active RhoA.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on known roles of RhoA.

claim: Active RhoA would drive arc formation by simultaneously targeting, unfolding, and activating mDia1 at the plasma membrane.
source: First, active RhoA would drive arc formation by simultaneously targeting, unfolding, and activating mDia1 at the plasma membrane (Kühn and Geyer, 2014; Rose et al., 2005).
